title: Analysis of Household Contact Investigation Data to Inform Development of Clinical Prediction Models for Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis in Rural Eastern Cape, South Africa
content: Background: Early identification of individuals at heightened risk for drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) is essential for prioritising rapid diagnostic testing and targeted preventive care, particularly in resource-constrained rural settings. Although routine tuberculosis (TB) surveillance and household contact investigation records provide an accessible data source, their predictive capacity and utility for machine learning-based risk stratification remain under-evaluated. This study evaluated the predictive utility of routine demographic and household contact investigation data for programme-defined risk classification in rural Eastern Cape, South Africa, and identified critical data gaps relevant to the future development of clinically actionable DR-TB prediction models. Methods: A retrospective secondary analysis was conducted using anonymised, routinely collected household contact investigation data from 437 contacts of smear-positive pulmonary TB index cases in King Sabata Dalindyebo Municipality, Eastern Cape. The primary outcome was programme-assigned TB vulnerability classification (high versus low risk), rather than microbiologically confirmed TB or DR-TB. Bivariate analyses and multivariable logistic regression were used to assess factors associated with high-risk classification. Three supervised machine learning algorithms—logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting—were evaluated using an 80:20 stratified training–test split and five-fold cross-validation. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), area under the precision–recall curve (AUPRC), calibration measures, and decision curve analysis. A structured variable-gap assessment identified additional clinical, microbiological, and molecular predictors required for future DR-TB prediction. Results: Of 437 household contacts, 290 (66.4%) were classified as high risk and 147 (33.6%) as low risk. Age was significantly associated with programme-defined risk classification (χ² = 16.61, p = 0.005), whereas sex was not. Children aged 0–4 years had the highest proportion classified as high risk (35/41; 85.4%). In multivariable logistic regression, younger age (adjusted OR [aOR] = 2.41; 95% CI: 1.48–3.94) and larger household size (aOR = 1.12 per additional household member; 95% CI: 1.01–1.25) were independently associated with high-risk classification. Gradient boosting demonstrated the strongest cross-validated performance (AUROC = 0.657, SD = 0.052; AUPRC = 0.785, SD = 0.042), although overall discrimination remained modest. Household-level analyses demonstrated clustering of programme-defined vulnerability. The variable-gap assessment identified important unavailable predictors, including previous TB treatment, HIV status, diabetes, microbiological measures, molecular diagnostic results, and drug-susceptibility information. Conclusions: Routine household contact investigation data provide measurable but limited predictive information for programme-defined TB vulnerability, with age and household size emerging as important baseline factors. However, these data should not be interpreted as directly predicting microbiologically confirmed DR-TB. Development of robust and clinically meaningful DR-TB prediction models in rural African settings will require integration of routine programme data with clinical characteristics, molecular diagnostic results, and drug-susceptibility testing, followed by appropriate internal and external validation.
